title: Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body

concept.text: The proposed innovation is surgery that removes diseased internal tissue and restores the function of the remaining structures entirely from outside the body, without an instrument crossing skin or mucosa. Examples would include removing a bowel segment and joining its ends, or reconstructing a blood vessel so that it remains open and carries blood. The defining capability combines controlled tissue removal with functional reconstruction; destroying a target alone does not complete it.

Noninvasive histotripsy provides a demonstrated starting point: focused ultrasound produces cavitation that mechanically breaks down tissue at a focal point, and clinical trials have demonstrated destruction of selected liver tumors. Extending this destructive capability to controlled resection, tissue positioning, secure joining, and confirmation of restored function is the proposed advance. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate those reconstructive capabilities, but it also does not establish that every possible external reconstructive method is unavailable.

significance.text: Conditional significance: successful external resection and reconstruction would allow operations without creating a surgical instrument access tract. It would therefore avoid injuries attributable to creating that tract, including incision-related hernias and instrument-track injury. The revolutionary step would be extending an access advantage already demonstrated for selected tumor destruction to operations that must restore continuity and function after tissue removal.

This would not make surgery wound-free. Resection and joining still injure internal tissue, and bleeding, infection, leakage, impaired healing, and damage to adjacent structures would remain outcomes requiring direct assessment. Even existing incisionless histotripsy can cause bleeding or infection where tissue is destroyed. Avoiding the access tract therefore cannot by itself establish lower overall operative risk, faster recovery, or superior long-term outcomes.

Further possibilities are conditional synthesis: access-free reconstruction might expand treatment options where creating an operative route adds substantial difficulty or injury. Preserving an infiltrated critical structure by rebuilding around it would demand additional precision, tissue discrimination, and reconstructive control. Neither cell-by-cell selectivity nor autonomous operation follows automatically from incisionlessness, and an achieved result in one accessible organ would not establish the same capability throughout the body.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability in the supplied evidence is the constructive half of external surgery. The retained histotripsy evidence concerns focal tissue breakdown and tumor destruction; it does not demonstrate retraction, suturing, reliable bowel or vascular anastomosis, or verification of a completed reconstruction performed entirely from outside the body. This is a boundary of the evidence provided, rather than proof that all mechanical tissue separation or joining universally requires an instrument at the site.

Engineering synthesis: a working system would need to control what is separated, preserve intended tissue boundaries, manage the removed or disrupted material, position the structures to be joined, and create a connection that tolerates physiological pressure and motion. Bowel reconstruction would require a sealed, viable join; vascular reconstruction would require a connection that remains open and supports flow. The innovation need not literally place sutures, but any alternative joining mechanism would have to demonstrate these functions.

Engineering synthesis: guidance and feedback would need to establish where treatment is occurring, whether neighboring structures remain intact, and whether the reconstructed structure functions immediately and during healing. Confirmation of a reconstructive result is a proposed requirement, not a capability assessed by the supplied ablation studies. The system would also need a defined response to bleeding, incomplete separation, failed alignment, or an inadequate join, including when conventional rescue becomes necessary.

Energy delivery also has practical boundaries. The Cleveland Clinic description identifies restrictions related to tumor size and acoustic access, so external treatment cannot be assumed to reach every internal target effectively. Extending treatment to reconstruction would require demonstrating reliable targeting and control within explicitly defined anatomical conditions. The packet does not establish a particular treatment-head depth limit or show how these access constraints would be solved.

current_state.text: The #HOPE4LIVER report, published online September 3, 2024, describes prospective single-arm trials treating 44 participants with 49 primary or metastatic liver tumors. The mean maximum pretreatment tumor diameter was 1.5 cm ± 0.6, and eligibility allowed treatment of up to three tumors smaller than 3 cm. These results establish a clinical demonstration in a selected tumor population, rather than unrestricted treatment of liver disease.

Technical success was reported for 42 of 44 evaluated tumors, or 95%, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 84–100%. Major procedure-related complications occurred in 3 of 44 participants, or 7%, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 2–18%. Both endpoints met their prespecified performance goals. The 49 tumors treated overall and the 44 tumors used for the technical-success calculation are distinct denominators and should not be conflated.

The retained PubMed material provides the abstract and captions, rather than the full trial paper. The abstract reports assessments through 30 days, and the single-arm design supplies no concurrent comparative treatment group. These findings support early technical success and the reported complication outcome; they do not establish comparative efficacy, durable cancer control, or reconstructive capability. The supplied material does not explain the difference between the total treated-tumor count and the technical-success denominator.

A Cleveland Clinic patient-information page updated September 28, 2025 describes histotripsy as local tumor destruction without incisions and discusses size and acoustic-access restrictions. It reports an FDA action for liver tumors in October 2023, using the word approval. Because this is a secondary patient-information source and the regulatory documentation is not supplied, the precise designation of approval versus clearance remains unresolved. The page also mentions one-year follow-up, but the underlying follow-up report is not supplied; it would therefore be inaccurate to characterize all later evidence simply as short follow-up.

The research also cites a 2016 randomized trial of focused ultrasound thalamotomy for essential tremor, reporting 76 patients and a transcranial procedure without incision or craniotomy. However, the source index contains no captured document for that paper, and the supplied review could not verify those statements from retained text. They remain attributed research claims here. Even if verified, lesioning a brain target would demonstrate tissue destruction, not internal resection followed by reconstruction.

The supplied sources do not demonstrate incisionless bowel anastomosis or formal vascular reconstruction. They also do not provide a bounded search establishing the absence of such capabilities through November 1, 2026. No supplied 2026 report verifies the broader contemporary landscape, and the asserted investigational status of kidney, pancreatic, and intracranial histotripsy applications remains unverified in this packet. These limitations leave present-day completeness uncertain without negating the supported historical liver-ablation results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in a survival large-animal study, complete either segmental bowel resection with a leak-free anastomosis or vascular resection and reconstruction with documented patency, with no instrument crossing skin or mucosa. The procedure should document both tissue removal and restoration of function. Tumor ablation alone would not meet this proposed scope. These are proposed benchmarks for the innovation, not established standards or reported achievements.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: compare leak, patency where applicable, and complication outcomes with the corresponding open operation using prespecified comparison margins, adequate sample sizes, defined endpoints, and follow-up long enough to assess healing and functional durability. The earlier phrase 'in the range' is insufficient without those choices. Rescue procedures, incomplete reconstructions, and departures from the access restriction should be reported explicitly, with survival and function assessed beyond immediate procedural completion.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed evaluation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: repeat successful operations across independent teams and report the anatomical conditions, target sizes and depths, delivery access, and disease settings in which the method works or fails. A convincing demonstration should include preservation of adjacent critical structures and reliable confirmation of the reconstructed result. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality across organs, patients, or operations.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical progression: after reproducible preclinical reconstruction, a first human feasibility case would mark an initial clinical step, followed by studies assessing repeatability, durable function, complications, and comparative outcomes. A single successful case would establish feasibility in that case, rather than broad safety or equivalence to established surgery.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed clinical progression

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SUR-06, Autonomous completion of whole operations at expert level, concerns who or what controls the operation; SUR-07 concerns how internal resection and reconstruction are accomplished without an instrument access tract. External surgery could remain clinician-controlled, while an autonomous operation could still use conventional incisions. The capabilities could be combined but remain separate advances.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-10, Cell-identity-selective extirpation inside an organ that keeps working, concerns discrimination among cells and preservation of ongoing organ function. SUR-07 does not inherently require cell-level discrimination. SUR-11, Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field, could support precise targeting and feedback for external reconstruction, but improved vision alone would not supply tissue manipulation, joining, or durable healing.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-05, Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis, addresses the biological outcome of injury. SUR-07 removes the need for an operative access tract while still creating internal injuries during resection and joining. Regenerative healing could improve those outcomes, but incisionlessness does not establish regeneration or freedom from internal scarring.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply, and SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation, concern production of replacement tissue or organs. SUR-07 concerns performing removal and functional reconstruction within the closed body. Integrating replacement tissue might eventually intersect with it, but creating a replacement does not demonstrate incisionless delivery, attachment, or connection to circulation.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive; SUR-02, Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation; and SUR-03, Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs, address transplant acceptance, organ supply, and preservation. SUR-04, Restoration of volitional function after complete spinal cord transection, addresses neural recovery, while SUR-08, Reversible metabolic arrest after traumatic exsanguination cardiac arrest, addresses survival and recovery after catastrophic circulatory loss. These could intersect with future surgical care, but none by itself establishes external resection and reconstruction, and SUR-07 does not imply their achievement.

change_log.change: Preserved SUR-07's identity and centered the definition on tissue removal followed by functional reconstruction.
change_log.reason: The concept's distinguishing advance is constructive surgery inside the closed body, beyond demonstrated focal ablation.

change_log.change: Replaced universal assertions about required physical tools and unavailable reconstruction with explicit limits of the supplied evidence.
change_log.reason: The sources examine ablation and cannot establish the absence of every external reconstructive method.

change_log.change: Narrowed the claimed benefit from surgery without wounds to avoidance of access-tract injuries.
change_log.reason: Internal resection and anastomosis still cause tissue injury and can involve bleeding, infection, leakage, and healing complications.

change_log.change: Preserved the trial's quantitative results, added confidence intervals and eligibility scope, and separated participant and tumor denominators.
change_log.reason: The retained abstract supports these details; 49 treated tumors must not be substituted for the 44-tumor technical-success denominator.

change_log.change: Specified the retained trial material's partial coverage, 30-day assessments, and absence of a concurrent comparison group.
change_log.reason: These boundaries constrain conclusions about comparative efficacy and durability without invalidating the reported results.

change_log.change: Qualified the October 2023 FDA terminology and incorporated the secondary page's mention of one-year follow-up.
change_log.reason: The supplied patient page uses approval, regulatory documentation is absent, and its later-follow-up statement prevents a blanket short-follow-up characterization.

change_log.change: Retained the thalamotomy example as an attributed claim with an explicit capture limitation.
change_log.reason: The cited paper has no retained artifact; its reported enrollment and incisionless technique cannot be independently verified within this packet.

change_log.change: Removed categorical contemporary claims about organ indications, treatment-head depth limits, and absence of reconstruction through 2026.
change_log.reason: The packet supplies neither supporting contemporary reports nor a bounded search establishing those assertions.

change_log.change: Expanded completion proposals to include defined comparisons, healing follow-up, independent reproducibility, rescue reporting, and anatomical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These make the proposed demonstration assessable without presenting editorial thresholds as published standards or finite tests as universal proof.

change_log.change: Integrated distinctions across the supplied concept roster.
change_log.reason: Access method, autonomous control, cellular selectivity, imaging, regenerative healing, and replacement-tissue production are separable capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The precise October 2023 FDA regulatory designation remains unresolved without the relevant regulatory documentation.
The supplied abstract does not explain why technical success was evaluated in 44 tumors although 49 tumors were treated overall.
The underlying one-year histotripsy follow-up report is not supplied, so its methods, population, outcomes, and implications cannot be assessed here.
The cited 2016 thalamotomy paper lacks a retained artifact; its reported enrollment and incisionless-procedure statements remain unverified within this packet.
No bounded search record establishes the contemporary availability or absence of wholly external bowel or vascular reconstruction as of November 1, 2026.
Specific treatment-head depth limits and the asserted investigational status of kidney, pancreatic, and intracranial histotripsy uses remain unverified.

The proposed reconstruction benchmarks still require operation-specific comparison margins, sample sizes, follow-up durations, endpoint definitions, and anatomical inclusion criteria before use in a study.
